demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Weapons or objects used as weapons

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

vignette:
Valentina Reyes is a 43-year-old widowed Latina woman who works as a cybersecurity analyst for a mid-sized financial firm in Houston. She was referred for psychological assessment following a workplace wellness screening that flagged her PCL-5 score of 53. She came to the first session quietly composed, though her composure fractured more than once as she described the event that has reorganized her inner life over the past two years.

The incident occurred on a Saturday afternoon when Valentina and her husband, Marco, were returning from a farmers' market. An argument had broken out between two men in the parking lot, and Valentina, who had taken a self-defense course years earlier, moved toward the confrontation when she saw one man shove the other toward the ground. She had a folding knife in her bag - something she had carried for years without ever using - and drew it reflexively when the larger man turned on her. In the struggle that followed, the blade caught the other bystander, the man she had moved to help, opening a deep laceration across his forearm and severing a tendon. He survived, but lost significant function in his hand. Marco died of a cardiac event unrelated to the incident six months later, and the two losses - the guilt and the grief - became entangled in ways Valentina has struggled to separate ever since.

The memory of that afternoon is not intact. Valentina reports distinct gaps: she has no clear recollection of the moment the knife made contact, only the sound the man made and the image of blood spreading across a gray sleeve. She cannot reconstruct the seconds before or after, no matter how deliberately she tries. What she is left with instead is something worse - an emotional residue that arrives without any accompanying image, a sudden wash of horror and shame that overtakes her without warning and without the anchor of a specific memory to explain or contain it. She describes sitting at her workstation, deep in a routine audit, when the feeling simply arrives: the full weight of what she did, pressing down without a face or a scene attached to it.

Her work environment has become a significant site of exposure. Valentina's firm recently contracted with a federal agency, and colleagues have begun attending briefings where security personnel carry sidearms. The first time she saw a holstered weapon on a colleague's escort in the corridor, the sight reached back into the fragmented record of that afternoon and pulled something forward - not a clear image, but the grief and the guilt arriving together, sudden and disorganizing. She left the building early and told her supervisor she had a migraine. Since then, she has rerouted her morning path through the office to avoid the corridor where those briefings are held, and she has declined two project assignments that would have required her to attend on-site meetings at the federal building. A promotion she was tracking has quietly moved to a colleague instead.

Confrontations of any kind - a raised voice in a meeting, a terse exchange between coworkers - act as a similar portal. The sound of conflict pulls her back toward the parking lot in a way she cannot fully articulate, and the emotional intensity that follows is not a flashback so much as a flooding: grief for Marco, guilt about the injured man, and a formless dread that she is, at her core, someone capable of causing serious harm. She had come to believe this about herself in the months after the incident, and that belief has only deepened. What she finds most unbearable is the grief that surfaces whenever memory - however partial - is activated; it is not clean mourning but something compound and contaminated, the loss of Marco folded into the loss of her image of herself.

What finally brought Valentina to seek help was a moment three weeks ago when she sat in her car for forty minutes after a minor disagreement with a coworker, unable to move, feeling the full emotional weight of the parking lot without any image to attach it to. She is most afraid that the gaps in her memory mean she will never fully understand what she did. She is most hoping, she said quietly, to feel like herself again - or to find out whether that is still possible.
